name: Digital Twins for Experiments
title: Digital Twins for Experiments
answer: A digital twin for an experiment is a live computational model of a physical laboratory setup, its instruments, samples, and protocols, used to plan, monitor, and interpret runs. It covers wet-lab and dry-lab workflows, from plate handling and liquid dispensing to spectroscopy and sequencing, and can represent both the equipment state and the expected biological or chemical response. The twin is distinct from a static simulation because it is updated with sensor or instrument data as the experiment proceeds. In laboratory automation, the scope includes scheduling, error detection, and what-if comparison against a reference run.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: A digital twin for an experiment is a live computational model of a physical laboratory setup, its instruments, samples, and protocols, used to plan, monitor, and interpret runs. It covers wet-lab and dry-lab workflows, from plate handling and liquid dispensing to spectroscopy and sequencing, and can represent both the equipment state and the expected biological or chemical response. The twin is distinct from a static simulation because it is updated with sensor or instrument data as the experiment proceeds. In laboratory automation, the scope includes scheduling, error detection, and what-if comparison against a reference run.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The twin typically runs on a workstation or on-premises server connected to the laboratory's instrument control network, often alongside a laboratory information management system. It needs a data layer that ingests instrument logs, sensor readings, and protocol files, plus a compute layer for the model and a visualisation or dashboard layer for operators. Many implementations use containerised services and message queues so that updates from liquid handlers, plate readers, and incubators arrive in near real time. Storage requirements are modest for metadata but grow quickly when the twin records high-frequency sensor traces or images.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Building a twin starts with a structured description of the experiment: the plate map, reagent volumes, timing, and expected readouts. Engineers then fit a model, often a set of differential equations for kinetics or a statistical model of instrument noise, and calibrate it against historical runs. During a live experiment, the twin compares predicted values with observed values and flags deviations such as a missed transfer or a temperature drift. The work is iterative, with the model refined after each run to reduce false alarms and improve what-if accuracy.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: A digital twin inherits the access and retention rules of the laboratory's data systems, so raw instrument files, model parameters, and audit logs need clear ownership and versioning. Risks include over-reliance on a twin that has drifted from the physical setup, and the possibility that a flawed model masks a real experimental error. Provenance matters because a twin used to justify a result should record which model version, which calibration data, and which sensor feeds produced each prediction. Rights questions arise when twins are shared across labs or with external partners, particularly around protocol details and unpublished instrument configurations.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward twins that can propose changes to a running experiment, such as reordering plates or adjusting incubation time, rather than only flagging problems. Closer coupling with robotic schedulers and automated liquid handlers will let a twin act as a closed-loop controller for routine optimisation. As instrument APIs become more standardised, twins will be easier to port between sites and less dependent on a single vendor's data format. The longer-term goal is a library of reusable twin components for common assay types, so a new experiment can be assembled from validated modules instead of built from scratch.
